title: Do not rush ahead of Allah and His Messenger.
subtitle: Letting guidance lead before your opinion does

row.title: guidance first
sub: then my opinion finds its place

then: This surah taught the believers in Madinah the manners of faith. Some people used to say a revelation should come about this matter, or that practice should be allowed. {trap}They were running ahead, deciding before Allah decided.{/trap} Ibn Abbas explained it as not saying anything that contradicts the Quran and Sunnah.
now: Someone in the family group chat asks a question about faith. You type a confident answer in ten seconds, before you have looked anything up. Or you decide what Islam should say about something, then go hunting for support. {idea}Let the guidance speak first, then talk.{/idea}
old: I already know what is right here, I will check later if I need to.
new: My view walks behind the guidance, not in front of it, because Allah hears what I say and knows why.
try: Next time you want to state what Islam says on something, pause and check a reliable source first.

title: A raised voice can quietly undo good deeds.
subtitle: Tone toward the Prophet and what it reveals
then: A delegation of Bani Tamim came to the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Bakr and Umar disagreed over who should lead them, and {trap}their voices rose in front of him.{/trap} This verse came down. Afterwards, Umar spoke so softly that the Prophet ﷺ had to ask him to repeat himself.
now: You are reading a hadith someone posted, and you reply in all caps that it cannot be right. Or someone quotes the Prophet ﷺ in a heated family argument and you talk over it. {idea}Respect shows in tone before it shows in words.{/idea} The danger here is the one you do not notice.
old: How loud I am is just my personality, it does not mean anything.
new: The way I raise my voice around his words shows what is in my heart, and it can cost me without my knowing.
try: When a verse or hadith comes up in a conversation today, lower your voice and listen before you reply.

title: Lowered voices, tested hearts, a great reward.
subtitle: Quiet respect as proof of a tested heart
then: Thabit bin Qays had a naturally loud voice. When verse 2 came, he stayed home in distress, sure his deeds were lost. The Prophet ﷺ noticed his absence and sent word: {reward}you are among the people of Paradise.{/reward} The verse praises those whose quiet respect shows a heart Allah has tested.
now: You read a warning in the Quran and your stomach drops. You think of every time you got it wrong and decide you are beyond saving. {idea}The same passage that warns also promises.{/idea} Fear that makes you careful is good. Fear that makes you give up is not the point.
old: If I read a warning that fits me, I must already be ruined.
new: A warning that makes me lower my voice is part of how Allah tests my heart, and it ends in forgiveness.
try: Pick one place where you tend to be loud, a meeting or a dinner table, and speak more gently there today.

title: Shouting from behind the walls of his home.
subtitle: Demanding someone's time on your own schedule

row.title: no sense
sub: most of them did not reason

then: A deputation from Bani Tamim arrived in Madinah and called out to the Prophet ﷺ from outside the rooms of his wives. Al-Aqra bin Habis shouted his name to get him out. {trap}They treated his private home like a market stall.{/trap} The surah takes its name from these chambers, al-hujurat.
now: It is ten at night and you message your teacher, your imam, your manager. Then again. Then you call. Then you send a question mark. {trap}Their home time is not your waiting room.{/trap} The people who serve you also have walls and families.
old: If I need something now, they should answer now.
new: Respect includes the person's private time, even when my need feels urgent.
try: Before sending a late message today, ask yourself if it can wait until morning. If it can, schedule it.

title: If they had waited, it would have been better.
subtitle: Patience at the door, and mercy for those who did not
then: Right after scolding those who shouted from behind the chambers, Allah shows the better way: {idea}be patient until he comes out to you.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes it would have brought them good in this life and the next. Then the verse closes by inviting them to repent, because {reward}Allah is Forgiving, Most Merciful.{/reward}
now: You are in a clinic queue and you keep going to the desk to ask how long. Or you push a friend for an answer they are not ready to give. {idea}Waiting well is often the faster road.{/idea} And if you already pushed too hard, the door to fix it is still open.
old: Waiting is wasted time, pushing gets results.
new: Patience is itself the better result, and when I fail at it, Allah's forgiveness is still there.
try: The next time you want to chase someone for a reply, wait one extra hour before you do.

title: Check the news before you act on it.
subtitle: One unverified report can harm a whole people
then: Many traditions link this verse to Walid bin Uqbah, sent to collect zakat from Bani al-Mustaliq. {trap}A report came back that could have led to action against them.{/trap} Allah ordered the believers to {idea}verify news brought by an unreliable person{/idea} before acting, so they would not wrong people and regret it.
now: A screenshot lands in your family group chat: a shop owner, a neighbor, a cousin, accused of something terrible. Your thumb is already on forward. {idea}Who sent this first, and how do they know?{/idea} One tap can damage a name for years.
old: If lots of people are sharing it, it is probably true.
new: Before I act on a report, I owe the person in it a check, or I may carry the regret.
try: Before forwarding the next shocking message you get, find where it came from. If you cannot, delete it.

title: Allah made faith beloved and beautiful in your hearts.
subtitle: Why getting your own way is not always mercy

picture.label: What Allah placed in the heart

then: Some believers wanted the Prophet ﷺ to act on their opinions, like the report about Bani al-Mustaliq. {trap}If he followed their wishes in much of the matter, they would fall into hardship.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes he cared for them more than they cared for themselves. Then comes the gift: {reward}Allah made faith dear to them.{/reward}
now: You pray for a job, a marriage, a move, exactly on your terms. It does not go your way and you feel ignored. Later you see what that path would have cost. {reward}The love for faith you still feel is also a gift.{/reward}
old: If my plans were followed, everything would turn out better.
new: My wishes are not always my good, and even my love for faith is something Allah gave me.
try: Think of one prayer that was not answered the way you wanted. Thank Allah for one good thing that came instead.

title: Your guidance is a gift, not an achievement.
subtitle: Bounty and favor from the One who knows
then: After describing believers whose hearts love faith and dislike sin, the verse names its source. {reward}It is a bounty and a favor from Allah.{/reward} Ibn Kathir explains He knows who deserves guidance and is wise in what He decrees.
now: You see a cousin who stopped praying, or a colleague who mocks religion, and a quiet thought arrives: at least I am not like that. {trap}That thought forgets where your prayer came from.{/trap} {idea}Gratitude leaves no room for looking down.{/idea}
old: I am guided because I am the kind of person who chooses well.
new: My guidance is a favor I received, so I should thank for it, not boast about it.
try: Today, when you notice someone far from faith, make a short dua for them instead of comparing.

title: When believers fight, step in and make peace justly.
subtitle: Peacemaking that stays fair to both sides

row.title: stop his wrong
sub: that is how you help him

then: Sa'id bin Jubayr said the Aws and Khazraj once came to blows with palm branches and sandals. As-Suddi tells of a family quarrel over a wife kept from her relatives that turned into a scuffle. {idea}Allah ordered peace between them, made with justice.{/idea} Both sides are still called believers.
now: Two aunts stop speaking and the whole family picks sides. Two friends in your circle fall out and you hear only one version. {trap}Taking your side is easy.{/trap} {idea}Being fair to both is the harder, loved thing.{/idea}
old: In a fight, my job is to support the person I am closest to.
new: My job is to bring them back together fairly, even if that means telling my own side they are wrong.
try: If two people you know are not speaking, send one a kind message that opens a door, without taking a side.

title: Believers are brothers, so mend what breaks between them.
subtitle: One body, one building, one family

row.title: one body
sub: one part aches, all feel it

then: The verse closes the passage on fighting with a simple fact: {idea}the believers are brothers.{/idea} Ibn Kathir brings the hadith of the body that aches together, and the building whose parts hold each other up. The Prophet ﷺ clasped his fingers together to show it. {reward}Those who mend and fear Allah are promised mercy.{/reward}
now: Two people in your mosque, your office, your WhatsApp group, are cold to each other. Everyone notices and nobody says anything. {trap}Silence feels polite, but it lets the crack grow.{/trap} A brother does something.
old: Their quarrel is none of my business.
new: When my brothers are broken apart, mending it is my business, and mercy is promised for it.
try: Make one dua today, by name, for two people you know who are not on good terms.
